promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

learningObjectives.title: Types of radiation and nuclear equations

questions.q: What is the relative charge of a proton?
questions.explain: A proton carries a relative charge of +1, equal and opposite to the electron's -1.

questions.q: Two isotopes of the same element always have the same number of which particle?
questions.explain: Isotopes are atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

questions.q: Rutherford's alpha scattering experiment showed that an atom is mostly empty space with its positive charge concentrated in a tiny central region. What is this region called?
questions.explain: Most alpha particles passed straight through, but a few were deflected back, showing charge and mass are concentrated in a tiny nucleus.

questions.q: The mass number of an atom is equal to the number of:
questions.explain: The mass number counts the total number of nucleons, which is the protons plus the neutrons in the nucleus.

questions.q: A carbon-14 atom has an atomic number of 6 and a mass number of 14. How many neutrons does it contain?
questions.explain: Neutrons = mass number minus atomic number = 14 - 6 = 8.

questions.q: An electron in an atom absorbs electromagnetic radiation. What is the most likely result?
options: It moves to a higher energy level
It moves to a lower energy level
questions.explain: Absorbing electromagnetic radiation gives an electron energy, moving it to a higher energy level further from the nucleus.

questions.q: An alpha particle is identical to which of the following?
questions.explain: An alpha particle consists of two protons and two neutrons, which is the same as a helium nucleus.

questions.q: A radiation source passes through a sheet of paper but is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Which type of radiation is it?
questions.explain: Alpha is stopped by paper and gamma needs thick lead, so radiation stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium is beta.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is an electromagnetic wave with no charge and no mass?
questions.explain: Gamma radiation is a high-energy electromagnetic wave carrying no charge and effectively no mass.

questions.q: Which type of radiation is the most strongly ionising?
questions.explain: Alpha particles are large and highly charged, so they are the most strongly ionising but also the least penetrating.

questions.q: When a nucleus emits an alpha particle, how do its mass number and atomic number change?
options: Mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2
Mass number decreases by 2 and atomic number decreases by 4
Mass number stays the same and atomic number increases by 1
Mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number stays the same
questions.explain: An alpha particle removes 2 protons and 2 neutrons, so the mass number falls by 4 and the atomic number by 2.

questions.q: During beta-minus decay, what happens inside the nucleus?
options: A neutron changes into a proton, emitting an electron
A proton changes into a neutron, emitting an electron
A proton and neutron combine to form a helium nucleus
An electron changes into a proton
questions.explain: In beta-minus decay a neutron turns into a proton and a fast-moving electron (the beta particle) is emitted.

questions.q: A carbon-14 nucleus (atomic number 6) decays by beta emission to form nitrogen. What is the atomic number of the nitrogen nucleus produced?
questions.explain: Beta decay increases the atomic number by 1 while the mass number stays the same, so 6 becomes 7.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for:
options: Half the unstable nuclei in a sample to decay
All the nuclei in a sample to decay
The mass of the sample to halve
questions.explain: Half-life is the average time for half of the undecayed nuclei in a sample to decay (or for the activity to halve).

questions.q: What is the unit of activity of a radioactive source?
questions.explain: Activity is measured in becquerels (Bq), where one becquerel is one decay per second.

questions.q: A sample has an activity of 800 Bq and a half-life of 2 hours. What is its activity after 6 hours?
questions.explain: Six hours is three half-lives, so the activity halves three times: 800 to 400 to 200 to 100 Bq.

questions.q: After two half-lives have passed, what fraction of the original radioactive nuclei remain undecayed?
questions.explain: Each half-life halves the number remaining, so after two half-lives a half of a half, which is one quarter, remains.

questions.q: What is the difference between irradiation and contamination?
options: Irradiation is exposure to radiation from an outside source; contamination is having radioactive material on or in you
Contamination is exposure to radiation from an outside source; irradiation is having radioactive material on or in you
Irradiation only involves gamma rays; contamination only involves alpha
They mean exactly the same thing
questions.explain: Irradiation is being exposed to radiation externally, while contamination means unwanted radioactive atoms are on or inside the object or person.

questions.q: Why is a gamma-emitting isotope, rather than an alpha emitter, usually chosen as a medical tracer inside the body?
options: Gamma rays penetrate the body and can be detected outside it
Gamma rays are the most strongly ionising inside the body
Gamma rays cannot pass through tissue at all
Gamma emitters always have very long half-lives
questions.explain: Gamma radiation is penetrating and weakly ionising, so it escapes the body to be detected while causing relatively little tissue damage.

questions.q: Which of the following is a natural source of background radiation?
questions.explain: Radon gas released from rocks and soil is a major natural source of background radiation, unlike non-ionising sources such as phone signals.
